content.overview: A deviation investigation should explain what happened and reduce recurrence without forcing a root cause unsupported by evidence. Product consequence and process cause are related but distinct questions.

vocabulary.definition: Condition directly associated with an event without necessarily explaining why the system allowed it.
Underlying system factor supported as a meaningful explanation of recurrence.
Corrective and preventive action intended to correct a problem and reduce recurrence.

sections.title: Build the timeline and scope first
sections.body: Lot genealogy, equipment history, environmental data and observations define the event before cause analysis begins.

sections.title: Test competing causes
sections.body: Evidence should distinguish equipment, procedure, training, material and environmental hypotheses; uncertainty should remain visible.

sections.title: Verify CAPA effectiveness
sections.body: A completed action is not automatically effective. Follow-up evidence should test whether the intended control works and whether new risks were introduced.

workedExamples: Replacing a failed fan corrects the immediate condition; investigating maintenance, alarms and response explains whether recurrence controls are adequate.
commonMistakes: Naming operator error without system evidence.
Confusing product disposition with root cause.
Closing CAPA when a task is completed but unverified.
content.practicalApplication: Prepare an investigation with event statement, timeline, scope, evidence table, causal analysis, actions, owners and effectiveness checks.
content.summary: A defensible investigation preserves uncertainty, separates consequence from cause and verifies improvement.
